body: By noon the last exam block has let out, and everybody on the south side of campus who can get outdoors has. The sun is out over the Commons, low and white, and the lawn is still wet where the Brick’s shadow lies across it. People stand around on the grass with their blue books rolled up in their fists and their suitcases parked beside them by the handle, and up on somebody’s shoulders by the library steps a boy in a Santa hat is waiting with a ruler for a baton.

At twelve the Ferrer Tower gets through the Westminster quarters, off-key, and then the first notes of “Hotel California” come down out of the louvers one bell at a time, slow and lopsided: a rock song played on a hundred and thirty feet of concrete by somebody in oven mitts. The flat bell is in it. It falls on the end of every chorus, a hair under true, and every time it does the lawn cheers it like a field goal and the boy in the Santa hat brings the ruler down.

Theo is on the path in the camel coat with Laney’s pink carry-on at his feet, holding it by the handle at arm’s length, as if it might go off. Laney mouths every word with her eyes shut and her sunglasses pushed up into her hair. Margot, beside her in black with her arms folded, is not singing; on the chorus her mouth moves anyway, and stops whenever Laney’s eyes open. Kevin has the Odyssey keys on one finger and spins them on the beat. Yusuf has his last blue book under his arm and winces, on principle, at every flat note. Down by the path to the Lagoon, Priya holds a clipboard of checkouts against her chest and ticks somebody off it in time.

Lena isn’t far off, at the front of a knot of girls from the second floor, in the cardigan with a scarf wound twice around her throat. Through the second verse she has her face tipped up to the top of the tower — to the louvers, where the two of them stood in October at five in the morning, her on the high bells and him on the low. Her eyes come down off it, across the grass, and find him. She doesn’t smile. The chorus comes round, and when the flat bell lands on the end of it she hums the note along with it, low, and he’s near enough to hear that she has it exactly as flat as the bell. She goes back to the tower.

The bells can’t manage the last line, the one about checking out and never leaving, so at the end a few hundred people on the grass sing it for them, badly, and applaud the tower, and the tower goes back to being a clock.

journal.title: The Ferrer Tower
journal.text: A hundred and sixty steps. VIVOS VOCO · MORTUOS PLANGO · FULGURA FRANGO, around the biggest bell. I call the living, I mourn the dead, I break the lightning. One bell is flat. She says it isn’t. Thursday the fifteenth, at five in the morning, we played the Saints on it. Half of Anacapa turned its lights on. Nobody knows who. Margot’s following up for the *Tide*, from a minivan: the police log says one of them was laughing; the bass came in late twice. Nobody confessed. The last day of finals, at noon: ‘Hotel California,’ the flat bell and all. She hummed it.

s10a.slug: FRIDAY · 1:00 PM · DELGADO HALL, ROOM 412 → THE FRONT CIRCLE
body: Theo’s half of 412 went to Los Angeles yesterday by FedEx: three boxes and a garment trunk. (“I don’t carry, Costigan. I *forward*.”) What’s left on his side is what was never going: the TV, the espresso machine, Rosie’s two princes taped up over the desk, the garment bag over the back of the chair, and Nonna’s twenty, folded small in the frame of his mirror. Theo is doing a last slow circuit of it in the camel coat with his hands in his pockets, touching nothing.

He stops at the espresso machine. The Post-it on its flank has been there since Labor Day, gone soft at the corners, and over the fall it has grown a line at a time in Theo’s neat hand. The last line is in fresher ink.

body.title: A Post-it, on the espresso machine

body: “Malibu,” Theo says, reading down it like the specials. “Labor Day. A classic. The hold — my finest hour with a bursar. The library.” He looks at Jack over the top of it. “I lied to a woman in a cardigan, Costigan. I’ve been carrying that. And the van, tomorrow, quarter to five in the morning. I got you a window.”
Jack has woken up to that square of yellow from his pillow every morning since September.
Theo peels it off the machine and holds it up at shoulder height, a waiter presenting the check.
“I never leave a ledger open over the holidays,” he says. “Ledgers get ideas.”

choices.key: Theo held up the tab. You let him tear it up.
response: Jack doesn’t reach for it.

Theo waits to see whether he will. When he doesn’t, Theo tears the Post-it in half along the line under MALIBU, and in half again, slowly, and lets the quarters go into the wastebasket under the desk one at a time, as solemnly as earth onto a coffin.
“Merry Christmas,” he says. “Don’t be weird about it.”
On the foot of Jack’s bed, folded in a square, is the gray cashmere throw off Theo’s own bed. “For Ohio,” Theo says. “I’ve been. It’s cold.”
On his way to the door he slides Nonna’s twenty out of the frame of his mirror, folds it once more along its old crease, and puts it in his wallet. “For LA.”

Down in the front circle the SL is idling with the top up, the garment bag laid along the shelf behind the seats and Laney’s hatbox strapped onto the trunk rack. Laney is in the passenger seat in her sunglasses, with her two suitcases packed into the footwell around her shins. When Lena comes out through the front doors in the cardigan, Laney climbs out over the suitcases to get to her, and the two of them hold on to each other on the curb, swaying a little, Laney saying something into Lena’s hair that doesn’t carry and Lena nodding at it, for so long that Theo leans across and sounds the horn. “Go,” Lena says, into Laney’s shoulder. “He’ll leave you.” “He would *not*.”
Laney lets go at last and folds herself back in among the luggage, and from the passenger window she gives Jack the wave: wrist, wrist, elbow, elbow. “Every step, fireman,” she says. “I mean it.”
Theo is last. He leans across Laney to the open window, one hand on the wheel. “Have a good Christmas, Costigan.” He puts the car in gear. “All of it.”

The window goes up. The SL takes the circle and turns out onto Ocean Road with the hatbox riding high and pink on the back, and Lena, beside Jack on the curb, is still waving at the corner after it has gone round it.

journal.title: Theo Vance
journal.text: Roommate. Drives his grandfather’s car like a getaway. His father calls him Teddy and stays six minutes. Heard my brother’s voice and didn’t ask. Loves *Point Break* with no irony at all. Poppy texts him at midnight. The Big Sur Expedition, on his father’s letterhead. Called the Anchor and got my Saturday covered before I could say I work Saturdays. Bought six used copies of Kerouac off the cart at Driftwood. Halloween: threw the party of the year as Gatsby. Left it at twelve-thirty by the back gate. Found him at the wall at the Point at one in the morning, the second one. He said not there. Nineteen. His father sent a stretch Lincoln and a card that called him Teddy, and called at six minutes past and stayed four. His mother came up from La Cañada with Poppy. Blew out nineteen candles in one breath. Sunday night, to the ceiling: Laney says he asked if he could ask. ‘Like a vampire. They have to be invited in.’ He’s known since Friday. Wednesday I said I ended it. He opened his jar and gave me a spoon. Friday he took me to a party in Montecito so I wouldn’t meet anybody, and lost me in three minutes. Saturday at six he was on his bed in his coat. He’d called me nine times. At halftime of Michigan I asked him home for Thanksgiving. He said yes before I finished, and bought two tickets to Pittsburgh. ‘Guests bring something.’ Looked up St. Elizabeth’s visiting hours before I asked. Thanksgiving: came to Youngstown in Dad’s Browns parka over the camel coat. Dad said that’s not a coat. Speaks Italian from a movie, wrong. Rolled Nonna’s crust and made his own peach pie. Dad asked him to say grace. He did. Nonna asked who prays for him; he said nobody. Met Danny — Danny liked him in a minute. Didn’t talk the whole way home. Kept Rosie’s prince. Nonna gave him a twenty. Back at Marisol he reads me the News Feed in the morning like the intentions at the twelve-ten. Wants to know if I *like* things now. Says I’m fast. Says I’ve started sleeping with my phone. Played the Fishbowl a voicemail off the internet and ran one sentence of it twice: take your name off your phone. Timed my pocket with his stopwatch. Didn’t say the number. Taped Rosie’s princes over his desk; Nonna’s twenty is in the frame of his mirror. Covered for me at Alarm Five: I was in the shower. Sat on a dryer with Laney, discussing finals. Sunday at twenty to seven: back from somewhere. I asked him home for Christmas; so did Pop, in the garage. He has things in LA. ‘Tell your father I heard him.’ Put his cashmere on me Sunday. Said I was holding my phone like a rosary. Lent me the Burberry in the storm. Tried to heckle Julian’s song and couldn’t. Watched me go through Bastille’s window. Six in the morning on the last day of classes he asked why I look like I’ve been through a war. He had a question in his calendar for after Thanksgiving; he’s moved it. Sunday he filmed his shoes with a girl named Soledad. Tore up the tab. Left me his cashmere for Ohio. Have a good Christmas, Costigan — all of it.

response: “I’m paying the shuttle,” Jack says. “Forty dollars.”

He has it ready, two twenties out of his tips from the Anchor, folded once. Theo looks at the bills and then at Jack, and takes them. He crosses to the mirror, slides Nonna’s twenty out of the frame and tucks it into his wallet — “For LA” — and folds Jack’s two into the frame where it was, and stands back to look.
“Now I have a collection.”
He uncaps the pen on the desk, draws one neat line through + 1 SHUTTLE (SBA), and sticks the Post-it back on the machine. The rest stays open.
On the foot of Jack’s bed, folded in a square, is the gray cashmere throw off Theo’s own bed. “For Ohio,” Theo says. “I’ve been. It’s cold.”

s10b.slug: FRIDAY · 2:30 PM · ST. BRENDAN’S, THE MARIAN SHRINE
body: In the middle of a Friday afternoon St. Brendan’s smells of cold wax and the lemon oil Mrs. Fitch works into the pews before Christmas, and the blue glass puts the side aisle under water.

Jack has crossed Ocean Road with a dollar in his hand to light a candle for Nonna before the flight, and somebody has beaten him to the shrine. At the votive rack under Our Lady, with her oxblood Doc Martens planted on the tile and a long match going, Margot is lighting a candle in the back row. She gets it on the first try, shakes the match out, and sees him.
“For research,” she says.
He hasn’t said anything.
“If you tell Lena,” Margot says, “I’ll tell her you cried at Sully’s in October.”
“I didn’t cry at Sully’s.”
“She’ll believe me.” She tips her head at the iron offering box. “The sign says a dollar. I put in two. I won’t be accused of freeloading on the supernatural.”

He feeds his dollar into the slot of the iron box and lights one in the front row for Nonna, off the flame of a stranger’s. Margot hasn’t gone. She stands with the dead match in her fingers and her eyes on her own candle, as though it might be about to do something.

journal.title: Margot Lindqvist
journal.text: Margot Lindqvist. Has a folder on me. Called Lena and me useful idiots for Christian nationalism in front of four hundred people. Made a point about the Euthyphro I still can’t answer. Her mother teaches Classics at Reed. Held a wake for a cigarette on the roof and buried it at sea, for the prose. Had a brother. Her mother was forty-one; the test came back; they’d already picked the name. Anders. March 15, 2000. She’s defended her mother in every room since, and she defended her on the roof. Lena said his name. Doesn’t sleep. My friend. She has a faith column now, in the *Tide*, on a trial basis. If it’s boring they’ll kill it. She told me not to be boring. Came to Big Sur as an observer, for the monks — a functioning patriarchy in its natural habitat. Ran the *Tide*’s Ferrer follow-up from a minivan and wrote nothing down. Sunday at the coffee urn: ‘I’m not writing anything down.’ Halloween: Joan of Arc in duct tape, with her own haircut. Best Couple, with Pope Joan. She called it a category error and laughed anyway. Told me I’m surface acting. Hochschild, 1983. The flight attendants. On the stairs, about Julian: ‘He’s the healthiest thing in her life, Costigan.’ She meant it. Alarm Five: twenty-seven days; she’d said twenty-six. Out past one, four nights of six — she doesn’t sleep, she counts. Not writing it down. Sunday: UNEXPLAINED CITRUS. Nineteen on the solstice, four days early, under protest. Likes us. On the record. Lit a candle for research.

choices.text: Kneel beside her and say nothing.
response: He gets down on the kneeler under the rack. After a minute Margot gets down beside him, stiffly, the way you’d get into a canoe, with her hands in her coat pockets and her eyes on the flame. Out on Ocean Road an airport van goes by, full of somebody’s luggage.
She clears her throat. “This is excessive.” She doesn’t get up.
At a quarter to three she does up the top button of her coat, which was done up already, and goes. At the end of the side aisle she stops with her back to him.
“Merry Christmas, Costigan,” she says. “Sociologically.”
When he leaves, her candle is still burning in the back row in its red glass, with most of its wax ahead of it.
He finds a second dollar folded in his jeans, feeds it into the box, and lights one in the back row, next to hers.
“For whom?” Margot says.
“My brother.”
She looks at the two flames side by side in their red glass, and nods, and asks nothing else.
At a quarter to three she does up the top button of her coat, which was done up already, and goes. At the end of the side aisle she stops with her back to him.
“Merry Christmas, Costigan,” she says. “Sociologically.”
When he leaves, her candle and his are still burning side by side in the back row in their red glass, with most of their wax ahead of them.
“What’s the research question?”
“Whether it feels like anything.”
“Does it?”
Margot looks at the candle with her head on one side. “Inconclusive,” she says. “I’ll need a larger sample.”
At a quarter to three she does up the top button of her coat, which was done up already, and goes. At the end of the side aisle she stops with her back to him.
“Merry Christmas, Costigan,” she says. “Sociologically.”
When he leaves, her candle is still burning in the back row in its red glass, with most of its wax ahead of it.

s10c.slug: FRIDAY · 3:25 PM · DELGADO HALL, THE BIKE RACK → THE EAST STAIRWELL
body: By twenty-five past three the sun is low over the Grove and comes in flat under the eucalyptus, and the rack behind Delgado is down to one bike. La Flaca has it to herself: the rust, the wire basket, the seat that tips back when you sit on it, and Ray Ochoa’s clip-on light still on her bars.
Jack unlocks her and walks her round to the front, where Rafi is sitting on the steps with a duffel for his abuela’s between his feet and his skateboard across his knees.
“Boss.”
“Till Christmas,” Jack says, and holds out the handlebars. “It’s Christmas.”
Rafi looks at the bike, and at the light on it, and keeps his hands on his board. “Keep her,” he says. “My abuela says after Christmas a bike decides.”
“Decides what?”
“No stress. She’ll let you know.” He stands, swings the duffel onto his back, drops the board on the walk and pushes off toward the harbor, one foot and then coasting.

At the curb the Odyssey has its hatch up, and Kevin is fitting Yusuf’s bag in beside a case of water and a first-aid kit the size of a carry-on. On the back glass, in La Vang car-wash polish gone a little streaky in the sun, in Lena’s capitals: WHO DAT · 13–0. Kevin brings the hatch down and comes round the van and shakes Jack’s hand, and holds on to it.
“Respectfully, Jack,” he says. “Go home. Sleep. Tell somebody something.”
He lets go before Jack can ask him what, and gets in. From the passenger seat Yusuf lifts a hand. “Fourteen stairs.”
“Fourteen stairs,” Jack says.
At half past three exactly the Odyssey leaves the circle at the speed limit and not a mile over.

He walks La Flaca back round and chains her up in her slot. At 3:41 he’s on the landing between three and four in the east stairwell, where the bar is, and the building is quiet enough that he can hear a shower running somewhere far up, and the RAZR goes off in his hand.

journal.title: Skye Callender
journal.text: Skye Callender, two Ls. Wouldn’t give me a last name — said *Out* — till she texted it to me on the floor in Denver. Met her in a window seat in Montecito, reading O’Connor for a part and had the grandmother exactly backwards. Acts — since she was eleven. Starts here in January: spring, undeclared. She’s declared enough, she says. Doesn’t drink where there are phones. Drives a dented ’91 Saab she says is Swedish. It’s GM. Walked into the Pacific in November like it was a bath, and dared me in after her in my clothes. Asked to kiss me — out loud. She was the one who stopped, in the grandmother’s voice. Typed herself into my phone as SKYE (MISFIT), and called herself from it. Took ten hours to answer my correction. Work, she said — a carpet and a wall. Her car’s an orphan now, and it’s my fault. Nearly three hours at the Starlite, a truck stop up the 101, with Nonna’s pie on the table. Cast me as the Bible salesman. Wanted to know what believing is like — not what I believe. Wants me to miss her a reasonable amount. Get the window, she said. Kissed me again against the Saab in the lot. Slower. On purpose. She was the one who stopped — her thumb on my mouth. She’s on TV. *Sweetwater*, Thursdays at nine: she plays Cassidy, the nice one. Gina screamed. I explained GM to her. In her own car. Thanksgiving: texted me the whole drive from Pittsburgh. Spent it at her mother’s place in Studio City; the parrot says ‘momager.’ Told me not to watch her show. Wants me to be specific. We’re friends on Facebook now — one mutual friend: Theo, who knows everybody. Saturday night she called. Three hours on the porch. Made me do my family. Asked what Advent is. Asked if the TV part matters. Fell asleep in the middle of the Madonna. Monday she drove two hours from LA to sit in a car with me for two more, and set an alarm so she’d leave. Watched the President with the sound off and read his face like a script. Her phone learned a trick in September; she’s still not over it. Gives every truck on the 101 a whole life in three sentences. Knows every word of ‘Thunder Road.’ The tape deck finally let go of *Rumours*. Invited me to LA; I work Saturdays. Doesn’t take people home. Saturday, in daylight, on a rock above the tide pools: fractions, for the placement test. I drew her a pie. Sharks were a lie. I told her a saint broke in. Drove me to Burbank in the rain to be her cousin from Ohio. Everybody on a set wants something from her; she smiles for every phone. Plays a preacher’s daughter who forgives a thief. She played it dry. Washed a borrowed dress in a laundromat at one in the morning; it lived. Thinks the Immaculate Conception is the other one. Took the math test with forty kids and nobody looked at her once. Doesn’t take people home. Took me home. Lives on Del Playa, in a house with a darkroom she isn’t allowed in and two boards under the porch the boys won’t let on the rack — she’ll live there in January. On her bed I said no. She stopped everything and asked me why, and we talked till it got light. I told her it’s a no right now. She said she can work with that. Picked my present for the church party: a Magic 8-Ball. Every answer’s a line reading, she says. Her car died in Buellton; I pushed. She’s seen Our Lady of Guadalupe on every taco truck in the Valley and thought she was a brand. Friday night she took my ‘right now’ apart, point by point, with visual aids, and made a very good case. It’s still right now. I said no again, and she stopped right there and nowhere else. Came to the Anchor in my shirt; Gloria rated her boysenberry. She’s going to ask every day, she says. It’s in her calendar. Slept at her house. Just slept. She says that doesn’t happen. Taught me to surf at Ellery on Gaudete Sunday. I’m terrible. I go home in six days. She isn’t counting. Played Hale in her car from my description. Asked the one question I couldn’t answer. Thursday at one in the morning, on the darkest night of the year, she drove the bluff with the lights off. Not before Christmas, she said — Christmas and New Year’s and long distance are too much for something new. When I get back we’re dating. Officially. A whole thing. She counted. GM is killing Saab. I’m on the hook.

journal.title: Skye Callender
journal.text: Skye Callender, two Ls. Wouldn’t give me a last name — said *Out* — till she texted it to me on the floor in Denver. Met her in a window seat in Montecito, reading O’Connor for a part and had the grandmother exactly backwards. Acts — since she was eleven. Starts here in January: spring, undeclared. She’s declared enough, she says. Doesn’t drink where there are phones. Drives a dented ’91 Saab she says is Swedish. It’s GM. Walked into the Pacific in November like it was a bath, and dared me in after her in my clothes. Asked to kiss me — out loud. She was the one who stopped, in the grandmother’s voice. Typed herself into my phone as SKYE (MISFIT), and called herself from it. Took ten hours to answer my correction. Work, she said — a carpet and a wall. Her car’s an orphan now, and it’s my fault. Nearly three hours at the Starlite, a truck stop up the 101, with Nonna’s pie on the table. Cast me as the Bible salesman. Wanted to know what believing is like — not what I believe. Wants me to miss her a reasonable amount. Get the window, she said. Kissed me again against the Saab in the lot. Slower. On purpose. She was the one who stopped — her thumb on my mouth. She’s on TV. *Sweetwater*, Thursdays at nine: she plays Cassidy, the nice one. Gina screamed. I explained GM to her. In her own car. Thanksgiving: texted me the whole drive from Pittsburgh. Spent it at her mother’s place in Studio City; the parrot says ‘momager.’ Told me not to watch her show. Wants me to be specific. We’re friends on Facebook now — one mutual friend: Theo, who knows everybody. Saturday night she called. Three hours on the porch. Made me do my family. Asked what Advent is. Asked if the TV part matters. Fell asleep in the middle of the Madonna. Monday she drove two hours from LA to sit in a car with me for two more, and set an alarm so she’d leave. Watched the President with the sound off and read his face like a script. Her phone learned a trick in September; she’s still not over it. Gives every truck on the 101 a whole life in three sentences. Knows every word of ‘Thunder Road.’ The tape deck finally let go of *Rumours*. Invited me to LA; I work Saturdays. Doesn’t take people home. Saturday, in daylight, on a rock above the tide pools: fractions, for the placement test. I drew her a pie. Sharks were a lie. I told her a saint broke in. Drove me to Burbank in the rain to be her cousin from Ohio. Everybody on a set wants something from her; she smiles for every phone. Plays a preacher’s daughter who forgives a thief. She played it dry. Washed a borrowed dress in a laundromat at one in the morning; it lived. Thinks the Immaculate Conception is the other one. Took the math test with forty kids and nobody looked at her once. Doesn’t take people home. Took me home. Lives on Del Playa, in a house with a darkroom she isn’t allowed in and two boards under the porch the boys won’t let on the rack — she’ll live there in January. On her bed I said no. She stopped everything and asked me why, and we talked till it got light. I told her it’s a no right now. She said she can work with that. Picked my present for the church party: a Magic 8-Ball. Every answer’s a line reading, she says. Her car died in Buellton; I pushed. She’s seen Our Lady of Guadalupe on every taco truck in the Valley and thought she was a brand. Friday night she took my ‘right now’ apart, point by point, with visual aids, and made a very good case. It’s still right now. I said no again, and she stopped right there and nowhere else. I go home in six days. She isn’t counting. Played Hale in her car from my description. Asked the one question I couldn’t answer. Not before Christmas, she said — Christmas and New Year’s and long distance are too much for something new. When I get back we’re dating. Officially. A whole thing. She counted. GM is killing Saab. journal.title: Kevin Tran
journal.text: Kevin Tran. Goes to daily Mass, saves you a seat with a Bible. Has a sister, Tina, in dental school, who flossed in the womb. Lies to his mom about orgo in Vietnamese. Drives his mother’s Odyssey at sixty-five, not sixty-six. His dad has two nail-salon supply stores in San Jose and has never had a Labor Day. Brought six pairs of gloves to a beach cleanup. Mouthed every word of Joey’s first reading from the second pew. Somebody coached Joey; I can guess who. Brought tea to a wake. His Bà Nội says heaven makes the elephant and heaven makes the grass. Walked Margot down at four in the morning. Handed Lena a roll of quarters for the payphone before she asked. Halloween: All Saints, every one nobody’s heard of — scrubs, a halo and a white mask. He found Laney. Friday night a pre-med said Maine got it right. Kevin answered him and went to get water. Tuesday, the Vietnamese Martyrs: his mother reads eleven of the hundred and seventeen. Asked about the scar. Alarm Five, on the lawn: he had a question mark next to my name on his clipboard. I told Priya I was out. He erased it. Tuesday at four I woke him for Doug. A chair under the knob, then a bell. Wednesday at the Brick, at the next carrel all night: ‘You two have been defending each other for three hours. That isn’t studying.’ Sings bass. A real one. Seven years of Vietnamese choir in San Jose — his mother made him. Friday, from the Odyssey: Go home. Sleep. Tell somebody something.

journal.title: La Flaca
journal.text: Rafi’s bike, lent till Christmas. Not stolen. Abandoned. (A week’s difference, per his abuela.) Rafi won’t take her back. After Christmas, his abuela says, a bike decides.
